item.title: Hospitals deliberately targeted by Sudan's RSF fighters, BBC investigation finds
item.description:
Image source, Saudi Hospital medicsImage caption,
Medics at el-Fasher's Saudi Hospital performed a Caesarean by phone light on the day it was bombed ByBarbara Plett Usher, Africa correspondent and Mohamed MadiPublished1 hour ago
A BBC investigation has found evidence that Sudanese paramilitary fighters systematically destroyed el-Fasher's healthcare system during their long siege and subsequent takeover of the city in Darfur a year ago.
UN human rights chief Volker Türk called the findings "deeply disturbing", saying multiple attacks by the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) on civilian infrastructure, including health facilities, were serious violations of international humanitarian law and may amount to war crimes.
The RSF has rejected the BBC's findings.
The paramilitary group's health minister described the allegations as propaganda and a deliberate attempt by the national army and its allies to smear the RSF's reputation.
Using sources who were on the ground in el-Fasher, the BBC has found details of at least 43 separate attacks on hospitals and healthcare sites from May 2024 to October 2025 - some hit multiple times.
Under international law it is illegal to attack health facilities or their staff during conflict.
The investigation also reveals the toll on medical workers in the western city. In the period from April 2023 to October 2025, the BBC's data shows 120 were injured, 55 killed and 10 forcibly "disappeared" or abducted.
"The RSF [were] trying to evacuate the hospitals, to put them out of service because the health system is the cornerstone of any city or any state," says Dr Muhamed Suliman, a surgeon who was based in el-Fasher during the siege and spoke to the BBC.
"The RSF started hitting these areas so citizens have no longer any way to stay there. It was intense. It was deliberate. It was planned."

item.description:

Watch: Trump says Musk has restored Ukraine's Starlink internet access after rowByGabriela PomeroyPublished3 hours ago
Elon Musk has restored Ukraine's Starlink internet access, US President Donald Trump has said after restrictions hampered Kyiv's armed forces.
Trump made the comments after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said connectivity to the military-grade Starshield network, which is provided by Musk's satellite-based Starlink system, had yet to be fully restored.
Musk previously denied he was behind the slowdown, which affects Ukraine's ability to use drones to attack Russia and protect itself from attacks.
Trump refused to be drawn on a report that he had called Musk to ask him to lift restrictions to the service, but when asked about it he said: "Bottom line, he put it back."
The Trump administration previously denied instructing Musk's company to restrict access.
The connectivity restrictions came as Trump put pressure on Zelensky to stop attacking Russian oil refineries, which he has argued have caused prices to rise.
Faced with midterm elections next month, Trump has waived some sanctions on Russia and agreed a deal to import Russian diesel for the US market - a move which has been criticised by Ukraine and its European allies.
Image source, ReutersImage caption,
A Ukrainian soldier using a Starlink satellite internet terminal which connects to thousands of SpaceX satellites
Why is Starlink internet so important on the battlefield in Ukraine?
Published15 October
Ukraine uses both the civilian service Starlink and the more secure Starshield, depending on what communications are needed.
The networks use 10,000 satellites in low Earth orbit to provide connectivity, particularly in remote areas and battlefields.

item.title: Newborn twins fight for survival as conflict fuels Yemen's hunger crisis
item.description:
To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser.
This video can not be playedFigure caption,
Watch: Children in Yemen face homelessness and malnutrition as war ragesByOrla GuerinSenior International Correspondent, Reporting fromAdenPublished9 hours ago
From the day they were born, just seven weeks ago, twins Raghad Hassan and her brother Raad have been battling for survival.
They came into the world prematurely, as fighting surged in Yemen's long-running civil war between Houthi rebel fighters and government forces.
When the Houthis reached their village in the Kahboub mountains in south-west Yemen, their family of seven was forced to flee amid bombs, missiles, and drone attacks – the twins protected only by blankets.
What followed was three days on foot heading for the port city of Aden.
Image source, Lee Durant/BBCImage caption,
The twins' family walked for three days before being given a lift to Aden
"It was very difficult," says their father, Bajash Ali Sagir Hassan, a softly spoken shepherd. "We didn't find cars or transportation. One kind person brought us here [on the fourth day] while others refused."
As the family walked, the twins got weaker, according to their mother Lina. "They were exhausted… there was cold and dust. Their vomiting and diarrhoea got worse."
By the time the newly homeless family arrived at al-Sadaqah hospital in Aden, the twins were barely clinging to life. "Just skin and bone," said a doctor, shaking his head, as he looked at their wasted limbs.
Raad was the sicker of the two - his ribs visible and his chest heaving as he took rapid, shallow breaths. He was barely bigger than the hands of the nurse who carried him gently to be weighed and measured.
Bajash looked on, worry etched on his face. He told us the twins were fed twice a day, but sometimes he could only give them water - after the war drove up the price of baby milk.

item.title: L'Oreal says weight loss drugs are impacting beauty and skin care sales
item.description:
Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption,
The use of weight loss drugs, known as GLP-1s, has increased in popularity in recent yearsByRachel ClunBusiness reporterPublished2 hours ago
Beauty giant L'Oreal says the rise of weight loss drugs has affected beauty and skin care sales, as it designs products to specifically target some side effects of rapid weight loss.
The company's head Nicolas Hieronimus said the beauty market was proving resilient in a challenging global context, and that the use of GLP-1s was "a very important phenomenon for us".
He told an investor call that the rise in their use was "having an impact on beauty consumption and skin care consumption in particular".
L'Oreal, which owns other popular brands including Maybelline and La Roche-Posay, announced on Thursday that sales in the three months to September rose by 7.7%, above analyst expectations.
The use of GLP-1s has boomed in popularity in recent years, after drugs developed to treat diabetes such as Ozempic, Wegovy and Mounjaro were found to also lead to significant weight loss because they supress the appetite.
While it is not caused by GLP-1 drugs directly, rapid weight loss can, for some people, come with a side effect of loose skin - including around the face.
Hieronimus said L'Oreal's brands SkinCeuticals and Kiehl's have products "that have been designed to work alongside and complement GLP-1 and its side effects on skin sagging" and other effects related to rapid weight loss.
L'Oreal has also moved further into the clinical aesthetic space, increasing its stake in dermatology firm Galderma to 20% last December.
Both companies have been testing products on GLP-1 users worried about loose skin in separate clinical trials, according to Reuters.
Galderma owns popular aesthetic products including Sculptra, an injectable aimed at stimulating collagen production, and Restylane, which is an injectable dermal filler.

item.title: Trump ordered to answer questions under oath in BBC lawsuit
item.description:
Image source, Kent NISHIMURA / AFP via Getty ImagesByBernd Debusmann JrWhite House reporter Published22 October 2026Updated 50 minutes ago
A US judge has ordered President Donald Trump to answer questions under oath in his defamation lawsuit against the BBC by 11 December.
Trump is suing the BBC over an episode of Panorama that edited together two different sections of a speech he gave before the riot at the US Capitol in 2021.
Trump cancelled a previous deposition - or interview under oath - on 16 October, citing "matters of national importance".
But a lawyer representing the BBC said in court that Trump was campaigning in Georgia that day and had "prioritised that" over answering the questions.
President Trump's lawsuit against the BBC is in the phase known as "discovery", where the two sides provide internal or other records that could form evidence.
Charles Tobin, a lawyer for the BBC, told a court in Miami on Thursday that with two months left in the discovery period, Trump had still not completed a deposition.
The judge in the case, US Magistrate Judge Enjoliqué Lett, said that Trump must sit for the deposition by 11 December, unless the discovery period is extended.
In US law, a deposition is an out-of-court statement made under oath in response to questions, which is recorded for use in later proceedings.
Typically, depositions take place in a lawyer's office - rather than a courtroom - without a judge physically present.
Depositions, however, carry legal weight and take place under oath. They are recorded verbatim by a court reporter, and the transcripts can later be used as evidence during trials.
In defamation cases, lawyers for both sides are normally present for depositions.
Last week, lawyers asked that Lett compel Trump to face deposition after the last scheduled meeting did not take place.
On that day, Trump attended a midterms campaign rally in Dalton, Georgia and a fundraiser at his property in Mar-a-Lago in Florida.

item.description:
To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser.
This video can not be playedFigure caption,
How did AI discover the internet's massive cyber-security risk?ByTom Gerken and Liv McMahon, Technology reportersPublished7 hours ago
Organisations and businesses are still scrambling to update their systems after cyber-security flaws were revealed in a widely-used programming language, PHP.
Websites around the world were taken offline on Wednesday and Thursday after the developers of PHP said "critical vulnerabilities" were found in the back-end language, used in web development for decades.
Researchers warned the "severe" flaws could expose millions of sites using it to potential hacks if left unpatched - and the UK government was among those to take some sites offline as a precaution.
There have been no successful attacks reported so far, but experts say any impact may take time - even months - to become fully apparent.
Downing Street said on Thursday "some" limited government services "may be offline" while security work was being carried out.
"The information I have is that 32 Government services are unavailable and four are partially unavailable," tech minister Baroness Lloyd of Effra told the House of Lords.
She attributed this to having "largely resulted from precautionary measures taken to protect systems while security updates and mitigations are applied".
The government did not specify which services were taken offline - but it said no large UK public-facing critical services had been affected.
A spokesperson said work had already taken place across government to "identify and fix potential exposures to our systems and our experts are continuing to work closely with both OpenAI and international partners on this issue".
"But this does not mean they were hacked, and work continues to resolve any issues," they added.

item.title: Crowd of 50 beats foreigner to death in South Africa
item.description:
Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption,
Anti-migrant protesters in South Africa demand that all undocumented foreign nationals leave the countryByOndiro OgangaPublished8 hours ago
A foreign national has been beaten to death by a crowd of about 50 people in Durban, South Africa, police say.
According to police, the unidentified man, believed to be in his late 30s or early 40s, was first approached by two men by the roadside before being assaulted by a larger group. He was pronounced dead at the scene.
Police have launched an investigation into the murder, with the motive yet to be established.
The killing follows a wave of protests against immigrants in South Africa this year, some of which have turned violent. Earlier this month, shops and cars were set on fire in Durban, as well as Soweto, near Johannesburg.
Provincial police spokesperson Robert Netshiunda told the BBC they cannot speculate on the motive for the killing in Durban and that more information would be shared once verified.
'We have to prioritise South Africans': Anti-migrant movement blocks foreigners from healthcare
Published18 October 2025
The uniformed group targeting foreigners in South Africa
Published18 September 2023
The government has urged the demonstrators to act peacefully, while also accepting the need for immigration reforms. It says tens of thousands of foreign nationals have been deported or repatriated since it launched a crackdown earlier this year.
One of the groups behind the protests, March and March, had initially set a deadline of 30 June for all undocumented migrants to leave South Africa.
Several protests were held ahead of that deadline, with reports of attacks on people from other African countries.
These prompted several countries, including Zimbabwe, Nigeria and Ghana, to take steps to repatriate their citizens amid fears of further violence.

item.title: Germany target of 'intensive' espionage, Merz says after suspected Russian spy arrest
item.description:
Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption,
Chancellor Friedrich Merz says Russian intelligence activity in Germany remains 'at a consistently high level'ByMatt SpiveyPublished7 hours ago
Germany is the target of "intensive" espionage activity, Chancellor Friedrich Merz has said after a Ukrainian national was arrested on suspicion of spying for Russia.
Officials said the suspect, named as Vadym Y., had allegedly collected military-related intelligence from Germany.
Merz called the uncovering of the case a "success", but warned "let us not delude ourselves - the activities of Russian intelligence services in Germany remain at a consistently high level".
Several people alleged to be acting on behalf of Russia and other foreign powers have been arrested in Germany this year. Germany has been one of the leading European suppliers of weapons to Ukraine since Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022.
The German Federal Prosecutor General's Office said on Thursday that Vadym Y., as he was identified under German privacy law, had been in contact with a Russian intelligence service through an intermediary since at least July 2025.
It also said the Ukrainian man had collected information including "on the production of armoured vehicles, ammunition, and explosives".
He is due to appear before an investigating judge on Friday.
In January, a woman was arrested in Berlin suspected of gathering information for an intelligence officer at the Russian embassy.
Other arrests this year included a Romanian woman and a Ukrainian man accused of spying on an individual supplying drones from Germany to Ukraine, according to the prosecutor's office.

item.title: At least four dead after storm brings flooding to southern France
item.description:
Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption,
A car lies abandoned after severe rainfall in Saint-Mitre-les-Remparts, near MarseilleByHarriet WhiteheadPublished22 October 2026
At least four people have died in France, and one other has been injured, after flooding caused by Storm Adam.
The storm triggered widespread flooding across southern France on Tuesday, inundating streets and disrupting transport.
The deaths included two women aged 86 and 26 who were found drowned in a cellar in the Bouches-du-Rhône region.
Corsica was also hit by severe weather. Local media reported that a 4x4 vehicle was swept away by floodwaters on Tuesday - one of the occupants escaped through a window, but another man was found dead. Authorities have not released further details about the fourth death.
In the towns of Mouriès and Saint-Martin-de-Crau, between Montpellier and Marseille, dozens of residents were accommodated in emergency shelters after the floods hit. Officials said one person had been injured in that area.
Roads and train lines ‌in ⁠the area were also disrupted, Transport Minister Philippe Tabarot wrote in a post ​on X.
"The water has risen to unprecedented levels," Jacques Witkowski, prefect of the Bouches-du-Rhône department, said in a statement on Wednesday.
Witkowski expressed "a thought for all those who are in distress", adding: "We are mobilised at an exceptional level to resolve several issues."
Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption,
A local resident shows her house which has been flooded following severe rainfall in Saint-Mitre-les-Remparts, near Marseille
More severe weather is forecast in France, with Storm Austen - a newly named weather system moving in from the Atlantic - expected to reach the country's north-west.
France's weather service, Météo-France, has issued an orange-level wind warning for five western departments from Thursday evening into Friday.

item.title: Lula says rival should be disqualified over alleged Meta interference ahead of Brazil vote
item.description:
Image source, ReutersImage caption,
Left-wing incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva will face his right-wing rival Flávio Bolsonaro in the second round of voting on SundayByGabriela BoccaccioPublished7 hours ago
Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva's campaign has requested the disqualification of right-wing challenger Flávio Bolsonaro in the lead up to the final round of the presidential election on Sunday over alleged interference by social media company Meta.
In a petition filed to the country's top electoral court on Wednesday, the leftist incumbent president accused Meta, the tech giant behind Whatsapp, Instagram and Facebook, of limiting its content to boost Bolsonaro's campaign.
In response, Bolsonaro filed a petition seeking to disqualify Lula over what he said was the mass dissemination of government posts on WhatsApp.
The company has denied the campaigns have been treated unequally.
It comes after UN experts said on Wednesday that they were concerned about reports of discrepancies in the ability of each campaign to reach voters on Meta's platforms.
A report led by the UN's special rapporteur on freedom of expression said Meta must ensure a level playing field online during the election.
It cited incidents including "temporary interruptions of one candidate's campaign account; differences in audience engagement, user feeds, view counts and reach; restrictions on that campaign's Instagram posts".
"Information, including from Meta employees, suggests that accounts linked to one side of the presidential race were disproportionately curtailed," it read.
Meta has denied taking action to favour one side of the election and has said it would comply with an order from a Brazilian court to treat Bolsonaro and Lula equally.
Lula's campaign had previously filed a complaint alleging that accounts and content related to Bolsonaro were boosted.
